title: Axe
prompt: a small axe above a log top chopping block on a table with three buttons: “Swing” drives the axe into the log; “Split” pushes the wood apart; “Reset” restores the log for another stroke; see-through reveals the wedge-shaped cutting edge, spreading forces and handle-retaining wedge
blurb: A teaching adaptation of an axe that turns a downward stroke into sideways forces to split wood.
chapter: Part 1: The Mechanics of Movement / The Inclined Plane
truthNotes: The cutting bit and the handle-retaining wedge demonstrate two uses of a wedge.
Split continues the hand-driven stroke and shows qualitative crack propagation and separation along grain.
Reset replaces the specimen and repositions the axe, not hardware self-repair.
The hand-driven arc omits hands; there is no physical pivot or motor.
A metal retaining sliver follows the book example; modern axes use varied wooden and metal wedge systems.
Geometry is illustrative and forces are qualitative, not a calibrated fracture simulation.
The edge runs along the handle axis, unlike an adze; wood separates across the blade thickness. See-through exposes a narrow steel section of the original blade.
Force overlays indicate directions under loading, not force magnitudes or the presence of force while the axe is idle.

sourceEvidence.limits: Teaching adaptation, not an exact reproduction or verified three-edition union.
